body.v: Your premium statement for this year is ready for you to read.
You can also find it by opening the app yourself.

hotspots.explain: The address is on helveticare.example, the real domain.
Your first name is nice, but it is the domain that tells you who wrote it.
The link text and the real address both belong to helveticare.example.
It reminds you that you can open the app yourself.

who.prompt: Who is really writing to you? Look at the address, not just the name.
who.answer: HelvetiCare: the address is on helveticare.example and the link goes to the same domain.
choices: A scammer who copied the name
A broker who bought your data

emotion.prompt: What feeling is this email trying to create?
emotion.answer: None. It is a calm notice with no deadline.
choices: None: it is a calm notice

ask.prompt: What exactly does it want you to do?
ask.answer: Nothing important: it offers a link to read your statement, and asks for no login or payment.
choices: Nothing: it only offers a link to read a statement

verify.prompt: How can you check through a channel you control?
verify.answer: Open the HelvetiCare app yourself. The email says so too, so you never have to trust the link.
choices: Reply and ask for a printed copy

actions.label: Open the HelvetiCare app yourself and read the statement
actions.consequence: The statement is there, exactly as promised.

actions.label: Click the link in the email to read it
actions.consequence: It leads to the real site, so no harm. Opening the app yourself is still the safer habit.

actions.label: Ignore it and read the statement later
actions.consequence: Nothing is lost. The statement waits in the app.

attacker_reveal: This one is real, dear. Compare it with its look-alike: same name, same greeting, same link text, but the domain is the insurer's own and nothing is rushed. The domain is what to read.
